characteristics: Good design must push technical boundaries and provide new solutions.
dos: Prototype with new technology or APIs before committing to it; ship the new approach only once it demonstrably improves the task, not just the pitch; always seek new possibilities for expression.
donts: Repeat existing forms without providing new utility; don't chase innovation as marketing rather than user benefit; don't treat innovation as an end in itself.

characteristics: The primary purpose of a product is its utility (functional, psychological, and aesthetic).
dos: Prioritize functional criteria and user utility; ensure design makes a product understandable and useful.
donts: Ignore psychological or aesthetic utility; don't include features that do not serve the primary function.

characteristics: Design clarifies the product's structure and makes it self-explanatory.
dos: Make the product's function speak to the user; clarify the product's structure.
donts: Rely on complex manuals for basic use; require high cognitive load for simple interactions.

characteristics: Does not make a product look more innovative, powerful, or valuable than it really is.
dos: Be transparent and truthful about product capabilities and performance.
donts: Manipulate the consumer with unfulfillable promises or false representations.

characteristics: Back to purity, back to simplicity; "Less, but better." Time and effort spent should be short, simple, and fast.
dos: Concentrate on essential aspects only; strive for purity; remove any element whose purpose you can't state in one sentence; keep interactions short, simple, and fast with clear signposting.
donts: Burden the product with non-essentials or unnecessary complexity; don't add needless decorative parts or friction just because they seem harmless.

characteristics: The aesthetic quality of a product is integral to its utility and well-being.
dos: Create well-executed, beautiful, and harmonious objects.
donts: Assume beauty is secondary to function; treat design as just visual style without purpose.

characteristics: Avoids being fashionable and therefore never appears antiquated.
dos: Design for longevity in both build and style; use high-quality materials.
donts: Follow short-lived design trends or fads that lead to throwaway culture.

characteristics: Nothing must be arbitrary or left to chance; thoroughness and accuracy.
dos: Ensure every detail is functional and precise; show care in the design process.
donts: Leave loose ends or allow sloppy finishes in the final output.

characteristics: Design contributes to the preservation of the environment.
dos: Minimize resource use and pollution throughout the product lifecycle.
donts: Use materials that cannot be recycled or are toxic; design for a throwaway society.

characteristics: Products are tools, not decorative objects; design should be neutral and restrained.
dos: Keep design discreet; leave room for user self-expression.
donts: Over-design products to look like works of art; overwhelm users with loud elements.

characteristics: The design is useful and marketable to people with diverse abilities.
dos: Provide the same means of use for all users; make it appealing.
donts: Segregate or stigmatize any users.

principle: Universal Design: Simple and Intuitive Use
characteristics: Easy to understand regardless of user experience, knowledge, or language skills.
dos: Eliminate unnecessary complexity; be consistent with user expectations.
donts: Require high literacy or high cognitive load for basic navigation.

characteristics: Communicates necessary info effectively regardless of ambient conditions.
dos: Use different modes (pictorial, verbal, tactile); ensure high contrast.
donts: Rely on color or a single sense alone to convey critical meaning.

characteristics: Minimizes hazards and adverse consequences of accidental actions.
dos: Provide warnings, fail-safe features, and easy undo options.
donts: Design tasks that lead to irreversible or catastrophic errors if misclicked.

characteristics: Accommodates a wide range of individual preferences and abilities.
dos: Provide choice in methods of use (e.g., right/left handed access).
donts: Assume a single user speed or accuracy level; force a single interaction path.

principle: Universal Design: Size and Space for Approach and Use
characteristics: Appropriate size and space provided regardless of body size or mobility.
dos: Provide clear line of sight to elements; make reach comfortable for any user.
donts: Obstruct the line of sight; ignore wheelchair access or reach ranges.

characteristics: Can be used efficiently and comfortably with minimum fatigue.
dos: Allow user to maintain a neutral body position; minimize repetitive actions.
donts: Require excessive force or sustained physical effort.

characteristics: The top-line vision and competitive advantage for long-term sustainability.
dos: Tie each design decision to one measurable business metric (retention, conversion, cost-to-serve) before proposing it; revisit the roadmap each quarter against actual usage data.
donts: Don't greenlight designs solely because they're trendy; don't set strategy in a workshop divorced from real usage data; don't design in a vacuum ignoring business goals.

characteristics: Winning by solving a real problem better and cheaper than alternatives, not by matching a competitor's feature list.
dos: Identify the one thing competitors force users to tolerate, then remove it entirely; solve problems in a way that makes the competition irrelevant.
donts: Don't compete purely on price; don't add a feature just because a competitor has it.

characteristics: Verifying assumptions with target users through direct feedback.
dos: Use the Build-Measure-Learn loop; build MVPs to test market demand.
donts: Assume you know what users want; design without direct user input.

principle: Quality Performance: Prior Knowledge / Divergent Thinking
characteristics: Idea generation draws on precedent and deliberately produces many divergent options before converging, especially during creative exploration.
dos: Study 5-10 existing solutions or precedents before sketching; generate at least 3 genuinely different directions before picking one; apply existing principles as a starting point, not a cage.
donts: Don't lock onto the first idea that comes to mind; don't skip precedent research when time is short; don't ignore historical precedents in the name of originality.

characteristics: Layouts and components must adapt from small mobile viewports to large desktop or TV screens while keeping data and interactions consistent.
dos: Test key flows at both a minimum (~360px) and a maximum (1920px+) viewport width; use responsive or fluid layout techniques rather than fixed-pixel breakpoints only; ensure data integrity and consistency across all screen sizes.
donts: Don't optimize for one screen size only; don't ignore touch-target and reach constraints on small devices.

characteristics: Finding the core of an idea to make it stick.
dos: Strip away everything but the essential message; use analogies.
donts: Bury the lead; overcomplicate the message with needless data.

characteristics: Getting people to act through narrative and mental simulation.
dos: Use case studies; frame experiences as a hero's journey with a start and end.
donts: Just list facts without context; present data without narrative context.

characteristics: Using sensory details and actionable info to lighten cognitive load.
dos: Use specific, real-world examples and sensory language.
donts: Rely on abstract concepts, vague jargon, or high-level abstractions.

characteristics: Building trust through authority, details, or statistics.
dos: Cite one specific, sourced statistic rather than a vague superlative; show a real customer example or verifiable detail (a name, number, or date).
donts: Make wild, unsubstantiated claims; use statistics without a source or context.

characteristics: Making the audience care by appealing to self-interest or identity.
dos: Give the device a personality; use human connections and humor.
donts: Stay purely analytical, cold, or clinical.

characteristics: Grabbing attention by breaking patterns or defying expectations.
dos: Use surprise to spark curiosity; include "Easter eggs" or happy surprises.
donts: Be boring, overly predictable, or repetitive.

characteristics: Focus on foundational stability, reliability, and efficiency.
dos: Ensure core features like booking work perfectly every time; prioritize speed.
donts: Prioritize flashy/vanity features over system uptime and utility.

characteristics: Establishing trust through transparency and safety.
dos: Provide clear feedback, transparent pricing, ETAs, and safety markers.
donts: Hide critical data; use dark patterns; hide information that causes anxiety.

characteristics: Expressing brand identity and personality through design.
dos: Pick one signature detail (an illustration style, a motion signature, a voice quirk) and repeat it consistently rather than styling every screen differently.
donts: Don't copy a competitor's UI pattern wholesale when a distinct pattern would serve equally well; don't let 'consistency with the category' become an excuse to look identical to every other app.

characteristics: Transitions between states or screens should be fluid, unbroken, and preserve spatial context so users don't lose orientation.
dos: Coordinate simultaneous screen changes; use shared-element transitions to maintain orientation between views; keep frame rates high enough to avoid stutter.
donts: Don't allow stuttering, lagging, or janky transitions that distract users; don't use abrupt cuts or jarring transitions that disorient the user.

characteristics: Movement should feel natural and physically plausible - mirroring real-world weight, inertia, and expected timing - so it doesn't feel robotic or arbitrary.
dos: Apply realistic easing (ease-in/ease-out) and physics-based timing; relate animation velocity or duration to the interaction that triggered it (e.g. a faster flick settles faster).
donts: Don't use linear, robotic timing; don't create movements that defy spatial consistency or gravity; don't use jerky or disconnected transitions.

characteristics: Motion relates to the user's point of origin and environment.
dos: Animate elements from their touch/click point; adjust for viewport size.
donts: Trigger animations from random locations; use 'one-size-fits-all' motion.

characteristics: Design improves when real stakeholders and users react to concrete work-in-progress, not just a written spec.
dos: Run regular design critiques with stakeholders using working prototypes or personas; treat feedback sessions as a scheduled checkpoint, not a one-off.
donts: Don't rely solely on an initial requirements document or contract negotiation; don't treat stakeholder input as a single kickoff conversation with no follow-up.

characteristics: Great UI restrains color. A single accent carries emphasis; overuse of saturated color destroys hierarchy and reads as AI-generated.
dos: Use one accent color per surface for the primary action/emphasis; keep a neutral base (cool or warm grey); apply the accent identically across the page.
donts: Don't scatter multiple saturated accents; don't shift the accent hue mid-page; don't default to neon glows or AI-purple gradients.

characteristics: Pure #000 and #fff are harsh and flat; refined palettes use slightly tinted near-black and near-white for softer, more premium depth.
dos: Use an off-black (e.g. near-zinc-950) for text and an off-white for surfaces; give greys a subtle hue cast (cool for tech, warm for approachable).
donts: Don't use pure black text on pure white; don't use fully neutral greys when a tinted grey unifies the palette.

characteristics: Grey text on a colored background looks muddy. The fix is to let the background hue bleed through.
dos: On colored surfaces, use opacity-reduced white text OR a hand-picked lighter tint of the background hue.
donts: Don't drop a neutral grey onto a colored background; don't assume a grey that works on white will work on color.

characteristics: Shadows and elevation read best when tinted to the scene, not pure black. Overhead-light shadows fall more below than to the sides.
dos: Tint shadows toward the background hue; offset them more vertically than horizontally; use a fixed elevation scale (small=buttons, medium=dropdowns, large=modals).
donts: Don't use pure-black drop shadows; don't invent ad-hoc shadow values per element.

principle: Craft: Hierarchy by Weight and Color First
characteristics: Size is the crudest hierarchy lever. Weight and color separate primary from secondary while keeping most text at one comfortable size.
dos: Establish hierarchy with font-weight and text color; de-emphasize secondary content (softer color) rather than bolding everything primary; align mixed sizes by baseline; order elements in the sequence you want them consumed (top-to-bottom, left-to-right); keep font weights at 400 or above even for small UI text.
donts: Don't rely on size alone; don't let HTML tag level dictate visual weight (an h3 used as metadata should look like metadata); don't use font weights under 400 for small UI text; don't let every element compete for attention and create a 'wall of content'; don't make the logo the biggest element on the page unless it is the primary action.

characteristics: Constrained, hand-tuned systems produce consistency; open-ended choice produces drift and decision fatigue.
dos: Hand-pick a type scale and a spacing scale (steps >=25% apart, e.g. 4/8/12/16/24/32/48/64); pre-define 8-10 shades per color up front.
donts: Don't derive the type scale from a pure math ratio you won't use; don't reach for the color picker mid-design; don't tweak spacing or font sizes one pixel at a time manually.

characteristics: One type family (or a documented serif+sans pair) with same-family emphasis reads intentional; mixed typefaces read chaotic.
dos: Use one font family per project; create emphasis with italic/bold within that family; keep line length 45-75 characters; line-height inversely proportional to size.
donts: Don't inject a contrasting typeface for visual interest; don't default to a serif unless the brand/aesthetic is genuinely editorial.

characteristics: Adding whitespace after the fact always undershoots. Generous space signals quality and guides the eye.
dos: Start with too much whitespace and remove it; tighten spacing within a group and increase it between groups so proximity carries meaning.
donts: Don't pack sections to fill space; don't use uniform spacing that erases grouping.

characteristics: Borders add clutter faster than structure. Depth, background contrast, and spacing separate content more cleanly.
dos: Prefer spacing, a background-color shift, or a soft shadow to divide regions; use cards only when elevation communicates real hierarchy.
donts: Don't box everything in borders; don't wrap content in a card when whitespace would do.

characteristics: A single, locked corner-radius system reads deliberate; mixed radii read broken.
dos: Pick one radius scale (all-sharp, all-soft, or all-pill) or a documented per-element rule (e.g. buttons=pill, cards=16, inputs=8) applied everywhere.
donts: Don't mix rounded buttons in a square layout or square cards on a pill-button page.

characteristics: Polished products design the full state cycle, not just the happy path.
dos: Provide loading (skeletons matching final shape, not generic spinners), empty (composed, shows how to populate), and error states (inline for forms, toast for transient); add tactile active feedback (subtle translate/scale).
donts: Don't ship only the ideal state; don't use a generic spinner where a skeleton fits; don't leave empty states blank.

characteristics: Every animation should communicate something (hierarchy, feedback, state, continuity). Motion for its own sake reads as noise.
dos: Justify each animation in one sentence; split motion into productive (short, task feedback) and expressive (longer, significant moments); animate transform/opacity only; honor prefers-reduced-motion; show how new content relates to what was on screen a moment ago (shared-element transitions) rather than cutting cold; use motion to direct attention to the next task, not just to decorate.
donts: Don't animate because it looks cool; don't animate layout properties (top/left/width/height); don't exceed one marquee per page; don't add decorative animation that slows the user down or overloads them; don't use motion that distracts from the primary task or a 'jokey' indicator in a critical/transactional flow (payment, safety alerts).

characteristics: Repeated identical section templates (three equal cards, endless image+text zigzag) are a hallmark of generated design.
dos: Give each section a distinct layout family; cap repeated patterns (e.g. no 3rd consecutive zigzag); make grid cell count equal item count with real visual variation.
donts: Don't reuse one section template down the page; don't leave empty grid cells; don't render every feature row as three equal cards.

characteristics: AI-generated design has signature tells that cheapen otherwise good work; removing them is high-leverage.
dos: Use specific real names/logos over placeholders; write plain functional copy; label steps with verb-nouns (Install, Configure) not 'Step 1'; keep numbers real or marked mock.
donts: Don't ship generic names (John Doe, Acme), filler verbs (Elevate, Seamless, Unleash), section-number eyebrows, scroll cues, fake div-screenshots, emoji-as-icons, or em-dashes used as decorative flourish.

characteristics: The product's domain and constraints outrank aesthetic preference. Trust-, accessibility-, and safety-critical contexts override style.
dos: Match visual language to product type and audience; state a one-line 'design read' (kind, audience, vibe, system) before designing; let accessibility/regulatory constraints win.
donts: Don't apply a trendy aesthetic that fights the domain (e.g. heavy motion in accessibility-critical apps, AI-purple in fintech, dark-by-default for wellness).
